claim: LightR is comprised of two tandemly connected Vivid (VVD) photoreceptor domains from Neurospora crassa.
source: LightR is comprised of two tandemly connected Vivid (VVD) photoreceptor domains from Neurospora crassa (Nihongaki et al., 2014; Vaidya et al., 2011; Zoltowski and Crane, 2008; Zoltowski et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the composition of LightR and cites multiple references supporting this design.

claim: VVD is a monomer in the dark and forms an antiparallel homodimer upon illumination with blue light.
source: VVD is a monomer in the dark, and it forms an antiparallel homodimer upon illumination with blue light (Nihongaki et al., 2014; Vaidya et al., 2011; Zoltowski and Crane, 2008; Zoltowski et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references describing the light-dependent dimerization behavior of VVD.

claim: VVD dimerization is accompanied by a major flip of the N-terminal tail, bringing it close to the C-terminus of the other VVD in the dimer.
source: Dimerization is accompanied by a major flip of the N-terminal tail, bringing it close to the C-terminus of the other VVD in the dimer (Figure 1A; Vaidya et al., 2011; Zoltowski and Crane, 2008; Zoltowski et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural change during VVD dimerization with citations and references Figure 1A showing crystal structures.

claim: Two VVD molecules are connected via a flexible 22 amino acid linker (GGS)4G(GGS)3.
source: To connect two VVD molecules, we designed a flexible 22 amino acid linker (GGS)4G(GGS)3 which provides sufficient flexibility and length (approximately 25–30 Å when extended in the dark state) to accommodate the association and dissociation of the VVD monomers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the linker design and its properties.

claim: The flexible linker provides approximately 25-30 Å length when extended in the dark state.
source: To connect two VVD molecules, we designed a flexible 22 amino acid linker (GGS)4G(GGS)3 which provides sufficient flexibility and length (approximately 25–30 Å when extended in the dark state) to accommodate the association and dissociation of the VVD monomers.
evidence: The manuscript states the estimated length of the linker based on structural considerations.

claim: In the dark, the opening of the LightR clamp increases the distance between its N- and C-termini up to approximately 25 Å.
source: In the dark, the opening of the LightR clamp could increase the distance between its N- and C- termini up to approximately 25 Å, which should distort the native structure of the catalytic domain and thereby inactivate the enzyme.
evidence: The manuscript describes the predicted structural change in the dark state based on the design.

claim: Opening of the LightR clamp in the dark distorts the native structure of the catalytic domain and inactivates the enzyme.
source: In the dark, the opening of the LightR clamp could increase the distance between its N- and C- termini up to approximately 25 Å, which should distort the native structure of the catalytic domain and thereby inactivate the enzyme.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism for enzyme inactivation based on structural distortion.

claim: Illumination with blue light closes the LightR clamp and brings the N- and C-termini together, restoring the native structure and enzyme activity.
source: Illumination with blue light would close the clamp and bring the N- and C-termini of LightR together resulting in restoration of the native structure of the catalytic domain and recovery of the enzyme activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the proposed activation mechanism with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: LightR domain was inserted at position G288 in the Src catalytic domain.
source: Our previous studies demonstrate that the insertion of a regulatory domain at position Gly288 in the Src catalytic domain can be employed to achieve allosteric control of activity Karginov et al., 2010; thus we focused on this site for the insertion of LightR domain (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the insertion site with citation and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of LightR-Src in the dark show increased RMSD of individual residues within the catalytic domain relative to active wild-type Src.
source: Analysis of LightR-Src in the dark shows increased RMSD of individual residues within the catalytic domain relative to the active wild-type Src (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations with reference to figures showing RMSD data.

claim: LightR-Src in the dark shows strong correlation between the motion of residues in the LightR clamp and in the Src catalytic domain.
source: Analysis of LightR-Src in the dark shows increased RMSD of individual residues within the catalytic domain relative to the active wild-type Src (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and a strong correlation between the motion of the residues in the LightR clamp and in the Src catalytic domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggesting a possible allosteric mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis from simulations with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The lit state of LightR-Src exhibits much lower RMSD, closer to wild-type Src.
source: In contrast, the lit state of LightR-Src exhibits much lower RMSD, closer to wild-type Src (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The manuscript reports RMSD comparison from simulations with reference to figures.

claim: The lit state of LightR-Src loses the motion correlation between LightR domain and Src residues.
source: In contrast, the lit state of LightR-Src exhibits much lower RMSD, closer to wild-type Src (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and loses the motion correlation between LightR domain and Src residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports loss of correlation in the lit state with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: LightR-Src in the dark shows substantial deviation of the G-loop.
source: Interestingly, LightR-Src in the dark shows substantial deviation of the G-loop (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplements 1B and 3), a critical functional element of most protein kinases (Cowan-Jacob, 2006; Krupa et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript reports G-loop deviation from simulations with references to figures and citations about G-loop importance.

claim: The G-loop is a critical functional element of most protein kinases.
source: Interestingly, LightR-Src in the dark shows substantial deviation of the G-loop (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplements 1B and 3), a critical functional element of most protein kinases (Cowan-Jacob, 2006; Krupa et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites references establishing the importance of the G-loop in kinases.

claim: LightR domain regulates kinase activity via disruption of the G-loop.
source: This suggests a possible allosteric mechanism by which LightR domain regulates kinase activity via disruption of the G-loop.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on simulation results.

claim: LightR-Src construct bears a Y527F mutation that disrupts Src autoinhibition.
source: In this and all following experiments, we used a LightR-Src construct bearing a Y527F mutation (avian cSrc position) that disrupts Src autoinhibition and prevents its negative regulation by endogenous mechanisms (Karginov et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the mutation used in the construct with citations.

claim: LightR insertion in Src completely disrupts its activity in the dark.
source: Our results show that LightR insertion in Src completely disrupts its activity in the dark which is recovered in response to blue light to levels comparable to that of the constitutively active Src (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from in vitro kinase assays with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: LightR-Src activity is recovered in response to blue light to levels comparable to constitutively active Src.
source: Our results show that LightR insertion in Src completely disrupts its activity in the dark which is recovered in response to blue light to levels comparable to that of the constitutively active Src (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from in vitro kinase assays with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Illumination of LinXE cells expressing LightR-Src induces robust phosphorylation of endogenous Src targets paxillin and p130Cas.
source: Our results show that illumination of LinXE cells, transiently expressing LightR-Src, induces robust phosphorylation of the endogenous Src targets paxillin and p130Cas (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from cell-based assays with reference to figures.

claim: Cells expressing catalytically inactive mutant of LightR-Src (D388R) exposed to blue light did not show any increase in phosphorylation of Src substrates.
source: Importantly, cells expressing the catalytically inactive mutant of LightR-Src (D388R) that were also exposed to blue light did not show any increase in phosphorylation of Src substrates (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports negative control experimental results with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Blue light by itself had no effects on Src targets.
source: This demonstrates that the increase in phosphorylation is a direct consequence of LightR-Src activation and that blue light by itself had no effects on the Src targets.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the negative control experiment.

claim: Noticeable phosphorylation of Src targets occurs after only two minutes of light irradiation.
source: The activation time-course demonstrates noticeable phosphorylation of Src targets after only two minutes of light irradiation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports time-course experimental results with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The level of activity of LightR-Src can be regulated by attenuation of light intensity.
source: The level of activity of LightR-Src can be regulated by attenuation of light intensity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results showing dose-dependent activation with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Phosphorylation of known Src targets including caveolin1 (Y14), p130Cas (Y12, Y128, Y249, and Y287), paxillin (Y88 and Y118), p120 catenin (Y217 and Y228), and cortactin (Y421) was significantly increased in LightR-Src expressing cells exposed to blue light.
source: Phosphorylation of known Src targets, including caveolin1 (Y14), p130Cas (Y12, Y128, Y249, and Y287), paxillin (Y88 and Y118), p120 catenin (Y217 and Y228), and cortactin (Y421), was significantly increased in LightR-Src expressing cells, but not in control cells, exposed to blue light (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports phosphoproteomics results with reference to source data.

claim: LightR-Src-expressing cells exhibited a broadly distinct phosphoproteome dynamics from control cells following light exposure.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that LightR-Src-expressing cells exhibited a broadly distinct phosphoproteome dynamics from control cells following light exposure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports PCA analysis results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: LightR-Src-induced phosphorylation events were enriched for cell migration, cell adherens junctions, and focal adhesions.
source: Protein interaction network analysis along principal component one revealed that LightR-Src-induced phosphorylation events were enriched for cell migration, cell adherens junctions, and focal adhesions, all of which are processes known to be driven by Src activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports network analysis results with reference to supplementary figure and cites known Src functions.

claim: 'Early responders' exhibited a significant increase in phosphorylation as early as ten to thirty seconds after LightR-Src activation.
source: 'Early responders' exhibited a significant increase in phosphorylation as early as ten to thirty seconds after LightR-Src activation, further demonstrating rapidity of activation achieved by LightR-Src (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal phosphoproteomics results with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: 'Intermediate responders' show increased phosphorylation at the 1 to 5 min time points.
source: 'Intermediate responders' show increased phosphorylation at the 1 to 5 min time points (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal phosphoproteomics results with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Src autophosphorylation on Y416 was detected at 1 min.
source: Interestingly, we detected Src autophosphorylation on Y416 at 1 min, indicating that Src phosphorylates some targets before it even undergoes autophosphorylation.
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific observation from phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Src phosphorylates some targets before it undergoes autophosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, we detected Src autophosphorylation on Y416 at 1 min, indicating that Src phosphorylates some targets before it even undergoes autophosphorylation.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the timing of phosphorylation events.

claim: A group of 'late responders' were phosphorylated at 1 hr.
source: A group of 'late responders' were phosphorylated at 1 hr (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal phosphoproteomics results with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2 exhibited only transient increase in phosphorylation at 5 min.
source: A distinct group of proteins comprised of MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2 exhibited only transient increase in phosphorylation at 5 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific temporal phosphorylation pattern with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: ERK1 and ERK2 phosphorylation is mediated by upstream MAP kinase cascades and leads to activation of ERK kinases.
source: This phosphorylation is mediated by upstream MAP kinase cascades and leads to activation of ERK kinases (Bugaj et al., 2018; Toettcher et al., 2013; Cargnello and Roux, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing the ERK activation mechanism.

claim: Src only transiently activates specific MAP kinase pathways.
source: Thus, our data indicate that Src only transiently activates specific MAP kinase pathways.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the temporal phosphorylation data.

claim: VVD dimerization is reversible.
source: Since VVD dimerization is reversible (Kawano et al., 2015), we hypothesized that LightR-Src should become inactive when light is switched off.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing VVD reversibility.

claim: Incubation in the dark led to a significant decrease in phosphorylation of paxillin.
source: Our results show that incubation in the dark led to a significant decrease in phosphorylation of paxillin (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results showing reversibility with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: It took up to 2 hr for phosphorylation to return to basal levels after switching off light.
source: However, it took up to 2 hr for phosphorylation to return to basal levels, indicating the slow inactivation kinetics of LightR-Src.
evidence: The manuscript reports the time course of inactivation from experimental data.

claim: The I85V mutation reduces the half-life of VVD dimer in the dark from 18,000 s to 780 s.
source: To achieve faster inactivation of LightR-Src, we introduced an I85V mutation into both VVD domains. This mutation reduces the half-life of VVD dimer in the dark from 18,000 s to 780 s and thus should facilitate faster LightR-Src inactivation (Zoltowski et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the effect of the I85V mutation on VVD kinetics.

claim: FastLightR-Src shows much faster reversibility compared to the original LightR-Src.
source: Indeed, our results demonstrate that compared to the original LightR-Src, the I85V/I85V variant (FastLightR-Src) shows much faster reversibility.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental comparison of the two variants.

claim: Within two minutes after the light was switched off, FastLightR-Src showed a significant decrease in paxillin phosphorylation.
source: Within two minutes after the light was switched off, we observed a significant decrease in paxillin phosphorylation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: By fifteen minutes, phosphorylation reached basal level for FastLightR-Src.
source: By fifteen minutes, phosphorylation reached basal level.
evidence: The manuscript reports the time course of FastLightR-Src inactivation.

claim: Activation of FastLightR-Src leads to a lower p130Cas phosphorylation level when compared to the same activation time point of LightR-Src.
source: However, we noticed that activation of FastLightR-Src leads to a lower p130Cas phosphorylation level when compared to the same activation time point of LightR-Src (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison between the two variants with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: FastLightR-Src can undergo repeated cycles of activation and inactivation.
source: To test this, FastLightR-Src was activated for two periods of twenty minutes each, separated by ten minutes of deactivation. Our results reveal successful cycles of activation and inactivation as indicated by changes in phosphorylation of p130Cas (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results demonstrating cyclic activation with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Activation of Src leads to stimulation of cell spreading.
source: Previous studies show that activation of Src leads to stimulation of cell spreading (Klomp et al., 2016; Karginov et al., 2014; Kaplan et al., 1995; Cary et al., 2002; Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references describing the effect of Src on cell spreading.

claim: Cells expressing FastLightR-Src start spreading upon irradiation with blue light.
source: Our results show that cells expressing FastLightR-Src start spreading upon irradiation with blue light (Figure 4A; Video 1) and stop immediately when the light is turned off.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to Figure 4A and Video 1.

claim: Cells expressing FastLightR-Src stop spreading immediately when the light is turned off.
source: Our results show that cells expressing FastLightR-Src start spreading upon irradiation with blue light (Figure 4A; Video 1) and stop immediately when the light is turned off.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to Figure 4A and Video 1.

claim: Repeated irradiation of cells with blue light induced corresponding cycles of cell spreading.
source: Repeated irradiation of cells with blue light induced corresponding cycles of cell spreading; demonstrating again that the LightR tool can be used to mimic oscillation of kinase activity in living cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Illumination of cells expressing catalytically inactive mutant of LightR-Src (D388R) did not induce any cell-spreading.
source: Importantly, illumination of cells expressing catalytically inactive mutant of LightR-Src (D388R) did not induce any cell-spreading (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports negative control experimental results with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Inactive FastLightR-Src localizes in the perinuclear region and translocates to focal adhesions and cell membrane upon activation.
source: Also, we observed that inactive FastLightR-Src localizes in the perinuclear region and translocates to focal adhesions and cell membrane upon activation (Figure 4C; Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with reference to Figure 4C and Video 1.

claim: The change in localization of FastLightR-Src is reversible and correlates with activation/inactivation cycles.
source: This translocation is reversible and correlates with activation/inactivation cycles.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from imaging experiments.

claim: The change in localization of FastLightR-Src mimics that of wild type Src.
source: Notably, this change in localization mimics that of wild type Src (Kaplan et al., 1995; Chu et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing wild type Src localization behavior.

claim: Local illumination of HeLa cells expressing FastLightR-Src induced the formation of membrane protrusions within the illuminated area.
source: Indeed, we observed that local illumination of HeLa cells transiently expressing FastLightR-Src induced the formation of membrane protrusions within the illuminated area and caused polarization of the cell towards the light (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from local illumination experiments with references to figures and video.

claim: Local illumination of HeLa cells expressing FastLightR-Src caused polarization of the cell towards the light.
source: Indeed, we observed that local illumination of HeLa cells transiently expressing FastLightR-Src induced the formation of membrane protrusions within the illuminated area and caused polarization of the cell towards the light (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from local illumination experiments with references to figures and video.

claim: The effect of local FastLightR-Src activation was reversed as soon as the light was switched off.
source: This effect was reversed as soon as the light was switched off (Figure 5A; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports reversibility of local activation effects with references to figure and video.

claim: Cells expressing the catalytically inactive LightR-Src (D388R) did not polarize in response to local light irradiation.
source: Cells expressing the catalytically inactive LightR-Src (D388R) did not polarize in response to local light irradiation (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports negative control experimental results with reference to figures.

claim: FastLightR-Src translocated to focal adhesions only in the area illuminated with blue light.
source: Notably, FastLightR-Src translocated to focal adhesions only in the area illuminated with blue light (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Video 2) and relocated back once the light was switched off (Figure 5D; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with references to figures and video.

claim: FastLightR-Src relocated back from focal adhesions once the light was switched off.
source: Notably, FastLightR-Src translocated to focal adhesions only in the area illuminated with blue light (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Video 2) and relocated back once the light was switched off (Figure 5D; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with references to figures and video.

claim: Local activation of Src is sufficient to induce local protrusions.
source: These results reveal that local activation of Src is sufficient to induce local protrusions and demonstrate that LightR approach can be used for the regulation of kinase activity at a subcellular level.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the local illumination experiments.

claim: Src induced local waves of increased cell-edge velocity.
source: Our analysis revealed that Src induced local waves of increased cell-edge velocity (Figure 5E,H; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A); suggesting the induction of recurrent local contractions that slow down membrane protrusion.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of cell edge dynamics with references to figures.

claim: Inhibition of ROCK and MLCK perturbed the waves of cell-edge velocity and reduced the average velocity of protrusions.
source: Inhibition of Rho associate protein kinase (ROCK) and myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), major regulators of contractile machinery (Parri et al., 2007; Totsukawa et al., 2000), perturbed these waves and reduced the average velocity of protrusions (Figure 5E–J; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from inhibitor studies with references to figures and citations.

claim: Inhibition of ROCK caused significantly smaller average velocity reduction than inhibition of MLCK.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of ROCK caused significantly smaller average velocity reduction than inhibition of MLCK (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), consistent with its limited role in phosphorylating MLC at the cell periphery (Totsukawa et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of inhibitor effects with reference to supplementary figure and citation.

claim: Sustained local Src activity induces waves of protrusions that are mediated by ROCK and MLCK.
source: Thus, by applying LightR-Src, we demonstrated that sustained local Src activity induces waves of protrusions that are mediated by ROCK and MLCK.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the inhibitor experiments.

claim: The majority of kinases share a conserved catalytic domain structure.
source: Since the majority of kinases share a conserved catalytic domain structure (Fabbro et al., 2015), we inserted LightR switch into Abl and bRaf at a position analogous to the insertion site used in Src (Figure 6A), replacing K282 residue in Abl and H477 in bRaf.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing kinase structural conservation.

claim: LightR was inserted into Abl at position K282 and into bRaf at position H477.
source: Since the majority of kinases share a conserved catalytic domain structure (Fabbro et al., 2015), we inserted LightR switch into Abl and bRaf at a position analogous to the insertion site used in Src (Figure 6A), replacing K282 residue in Abl and H477 in bRaf.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the insertion sites with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Illumination of LinXE cells expressing LightR-Abl-GFP induced the phosphorylation of known Abl substrate p130Cas.
source: Our results show that illumination of LinXE cells transiently expressing LightR-Abl-GFP construct induced the phosphorylation of known Abl substrate p130Cas (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Stimulation of LightR-bRaf-Venus induced phosphorylation of its direct target, MEK1, and led to downstream activation of ERK1 and ERK2 kinases.
source: Stimulation of LightR-bRaf-Venus construct transiently expressed in LinXE cells induced phosphorylation of its direct target, MEK1, and led to downstream activation of ERK1 and ERK2 kinases at levels comparable with the constitutively active mutant of bRaf (V600E) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: FastLightR-bRaf exhibited significantly faster deactivation kinetics, with a half-life time around 15 min compared to approximately 3 hr half-life of LightR-bRaf.
source: This variant exhibited significantly faster deactivation kinetics, with a half-life time around 15 min compared to approximately 3 hr half-life of LightR-bRaf (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of deactivation kinetics with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: ERK2 shuttles in and out of nucleus upon activation/inactivation cycles of FastLightR-bRaf.
source: Indeed, ERK2 shuttles in and out of nucleus upon activation/inactivation cycles of FastLightR-bRaf (Figure 6D; Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with reference to Figure 6D and Video 3.

claim: The LightR approach can be applied to achieve light-mediated regulation of different protein kinases.
source: Overall, our data show that the LightR approach can be applied to achieve light-mediated regulation of different protein kinases.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experiments with multiple kinases.

claim: The variant with LightR domain inserted at D153 residue in Cre showed activation in response to blue light.
source: The variant with LightR domain inserted at D153 residue in Cre showed activation in response to blue light (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results with reference to figures.

claim: The LightR approach can be used broadly for the precise regulation of several types of enzymes.
source: This demonstrates that the LightR approach can be used broadly for the precise regulation of several types of enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the Cre recombinase experiments.

claim: LightR provides tight temporal control of activity with tunable kinetics.
source: The key features of this method include: (1) allosteric regulation of the enzymatic activity, (2) tight temporal control of activity with tunable kinetics, (3) local regulation of activity at a subcellular level, and (4) broad applicability to different enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the key features of the LightR approach.

claim: LightR enables local regulation of activity at a subcellular level.
source: The key features of this method include: (1) allosteric regulation of the enzymatic activity, (2) tight temporal control of activity with tunable kinetics, (3) local regulation of activity at a subcellular level, and (4) broad applicability to different enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the key features of the LightR approach.

claim: LightR has broad applicability to different enzymes.
source: The key features of this method include: (1) allosteric regulation of the enzymatic activity, (2) tight temporal control of activity with tunable kinetics, (3) local regulation of activity at a subcellular level, and (4) broad applicability to different enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the key features of the LightR approach.

claim: LightR combines all critical advantages of optogenetics in one tool.
source: Importantly, unlike other approaches, LightR combines all these advantages in one tool, thus, simplifying application of optogenetics in biological research.
evidence: The manuscript emphasizes the comprehensive nature of the LightR approach.

claim: The modular design of LightR provides significant flexibility in the selection of the insertion site.
source: This modular design provides significant flexibility in the selection of the insertion site and allows for specific regulation of catalytic activity without compromising key functions of the protein such as its interactions with binding partners or its native localization in the cell (Karginov et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript describes the advantages of the modular design with citation.

claim: LightR allows for specific regulation of catalytic activity without compromising key functions of the protein such as its interactions with binding partners or its native localization in the cell.
source: This modular design provides significant flexibility in the selection of the insertion site and allows for specific regulation of catalytic activity without compromising key functions of the protein such as its interactions with binding partners or its native localization in the cell (Karginov et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript describes the advantages of the modular design with citation.

claim: Activation of a LightR-enzyme requires low intensity light (0.6 mW/cm2).
source: Activation of a LightR-enzyme requires low intensity light (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, 0.6 mW/cm2), minimizing the phototoxic effects of blue light illumination.
evidence: The manuscript reports the light intensity required for activation with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The light intensity required for LightR activation is lower than the intensity used in other optogenetic studies using light-sensitive switches to regulate enzymes.
source: This level is lower than the intensity used in other optogenetic studies using light-sensitive switches to regulate enzymes (Dagliyan et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript compares the light intensity requirement with other methods citing references.

claim: The activation of LightR is limited to the blue light spectrum.
source: The activation of LightR is limited to the blue light spectrum, thus enabling its multiplexing with other red-shifted optogenetic tools or FRET biosensors.
evidence: The manuscript describes the spectral properties of LightR.

claim: Early Src-dependent phosphorylation of talin-1 at Y26 and Y70 residues was detected.
source: Our phosphoproteomics analysis revealed early Src-dependent phosphorylation of talin-1 at Y26 and Y70 residues (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific phosphorylation events from phosphoproteomics data with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Y26 and Y70 residues of talin-1 are located in the N-terminal F0 FERM domain.
source: These residues are located in the N-terminal F0 FERM domain of talin-1 (Bouaouina et al., 2008; Goult et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing the location of these residues in talin-1.

claim: When talin-1 is in the inactive closed conformation, the F0 domain remains exposed and is proposed to act as an early detector of changes in the environment.
source: When talin-1 is in the inactive closed conformation, the F0 domain remains exposed and is proposed to act as an early detector of changes in the environment (Bouaouina et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the function of the F0 domain.

claim: Phosphorylation of talin-1 on Y26 and Y70 by Src may represent an early step in the inside-out integrin activation mechanism performed by talin.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of talin-1 on Y26 and Y70 by Src may represent an early step in the inside-out integrin activation mechanism performed by talin (Vinogradova et al., 2002; Vinogradova et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a functional interpretation of the phosphorylation data with citations.

claim: Later phosphorylation (1–5 min) of proteins involved in formation of new focal adhesions and membrane protrusions correlates with the time at which cell spreading and increased protrusion velocity were observed.
source: Later phosphorylation (1–5 min) of proteins involved in formation of new focal adhesions and membrane protrusions (such as lamellipodin, p130Cas, palladin, tensin-3, cortactin, GIT1, and paxillin) correlates with the time at which we observed cell spreading and increased protrusion velocity (Figures 4A and 5H).
evidence: The manuscript correlates phosphoproteomics data with morphological observations referencing figures.

claim: Elevated phosphorylation of many proteins at 1 hr is indicative of oncogenic transformation processes mediated by prolonged activation of Src.
source: Elevated phosphorylation of many proteins at 1 hr is indicative of oncogenic transformation processes mediated by prolonged activation of Src (Hunter and Sefton, 1980; Sefton et al., 1980).
evidence: The manuscript interprets late phosphorylation events with citations.

claim: Continuous Src activity induces only transient activation of MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2.
source: Our phosphoproteomics studies also revealed that continuous Src activity induces only transient activation of MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific finding from phosphoproteomics with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Short term Src activation induces activation of ERK1/2 whereas prolonged activity triggers inactivation of this pathway.
source: This suggests that short term Src activation induces activation of ERK1/2 whereas prolonged activity triggers inactivation of this pathway.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an interpretation of the temporal ERK phosphorylation pattern.

claim: Protein kinases are often activated transiently and can undergo repeated cycles of activation/inactivation.
source: Protein kinases are often activated transiently and can undergo repeated cycles of activation/inactivation (Kholodenko, 2006; Purvis and Lahav, 2013; Conlon et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Roche et al., 1995; Hilioti et al., 2008; Jacquel et al., 2009; Kholodenko, 2000; Maeda et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references describing oscillatory kinase activity.
